code:
SELECT customers.name, COUNT(orders.id)
FROM customers
JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
GROUP BY customers.name;
acceptedAnswers:
SELECT customers.name, COUNT(orders.id)
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
GROUP BY customers.name;

SELECT customers.name, COUNT(orders.id)
FROM customers
LEFT OUTER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
GROUP BY customers.name;
LEFT JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
explanation: A plain JOIN only keeps customers that have orders. LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and COUNT(orders.id) counts 0 for those without orders.

prompt: This should return the second-highest salary but fails. Rewrite the corrected query (typing just the fixed line also counts).
acceptedAnswers:
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)
explanation: Aggregates like MAX cannot appear directly in WHERE. Use a subquery to get the top salary, then take the maximum of everything below it.
